overview:
In Jain cosmology, Mount Meru (also called Sumeru or Mahāmeru) is the golden cosmic mountain that stands at the exact center of Jambūdvīpa, the central continent of the middle world (Madhyaloka). It functions as the axial pillar of the three worlds (Triloka)—the lower world (Adholoka), middle world, and upper world (Ūrdhvaloka)—and serves as a key organizing structure for space, time, and the distribution of beings.

Meru is not a physical mountain in the modern geographical sense but a cosmological and symbolic structure described in great detail in the Jain Āgamas and later cosmological treatises. According to standard Digambara and Śvetāmbara cosmological texts, Meru rises tens of thousands of yojanas above the surface of Jambūdvīpa and is partially buried beneath it. Its body is divided into sections composed of different precious substances—earth, stone, diamond, gravel, gold, crystal, silver, and other metals—corresponding to different vertical zones of the universe. Around Meru are arranged concentric continents and oceans, as well as the abodes of various classes of celestial beings.

Jain texts emphasize that Meru is perfectly central and symmetrical. Jambūdvīpa itself is circular, and Meru stands at its midpoint, forming the reference point for the four main regions (Bharata, Airāvata, etc.) and for the movement of the sun, moon, and planetary bodies. The mountain’s terraces and peaks host divine parks and gardens such as Bhadraśāla, Nandana, Saumanasa, Sundara, and Pāṇḍaka, which are described as extraordinarily beautiful and are frequented by gods (devas) and other higher beings. These descriptions are meant to convey the ordered, hierarchical nature of the Jain universe rather than to provide a map for physical travel.

Across Jain traditions, Meru is treated as an eternal feature of the cosmos, not created by a god and not subject to ordinary destruction. Its dimensions and materials are given in highly specific numerical detail, which also serve as a framework for other cosmological calculations (such as lifespans of certain beings and distances between realms). While Digambara and Śvetāmbara sources sometimes differ in exact measurements or narrative embellishments, they agree on Meru’s centrality, its golden nature, and its role as the axis around which the middle world is organized.

In practice, Mount Meru also functions as a powerful symbol. Jain temple architecture, cosmological diagrams (such as Jambūdvīpa yantras), and educational illustrations often depict Meru as a tall, golden, slightly tapering pillar or truncated cone rising from the center of a circular continent. For lay Jains, these images serve as visual aids for understanding the structure of the universe and for contemplating the vastness and orderliness of saṃsāra. Modern scholarship has compared Jain descriptions of Meru with Buddhist and Hindu cosmologies, noting both shared motifs and distinctively Jain features, such as the detailed layering of substances and the emphasis on non-creation and eternal cosmic order.

primary_sources.title: Trishashti Śalākā Puruṣa Caritra (Ajitanātha-caritra, Part 22: Description of Meru)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra (12th century, Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text:
jambūdvīpasya madhye meruḥ suvarṇaḥ sthāla-saṃsthānaḥ pṛthivyāṃ mūle sahasra-yojanāntar-niviṣṭaḥ, pṛthivī-tale daśa-sahasra-yojana-vistāraḥ, ūrdhvaṃ navati-nava-sahasra-yojana-pramāṇaḥ; trīṇi bhāgāni tasya, lokatraya-vibhaktaṃ śarīram.
ādya-bhāgaḥ śuddhā-pṛthivī-śilā-vajra-śarkarā-mayaḥ sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ; dvitīyaḥ ṣaṣṭi-tri-sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ suvarṇa-sphaṭika-aṅka-rūpya-mayaḥ; tṛtīyaḥ ṣaṭ-tri-sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ suvarṇa-phalaka-mayaḥ.
śikharaṃ vyāghranayana-maṇi-mayaṃ, caturaśīti-yojana-ucchritaṃ, mūle dvādaśa-yojana-vistāraṃ, madhye aṣṭa, agre catur-yojana-vistāraṃ.
primary_sources.transliteration:
jambūdvīpasya madhye meruḥ suvarṇaḥ sthāla-saṃsthānaḥ pṛthivyāṃ mūle sahasra-yojanāntar-niviṣṭaḥ, pṛthivī-tale daśa-sahasra-yojana-vistāraḥ, ūrdhvaṃ navati-nava-sahasra-yojana-pramāṇaḥ; trīṇi bhāgāni tasya, lokatraya-vibhaktaṃ śarīram.
ādya-bhāgaḥ śuddhā-pṛthivī-śilā-vajra-śarkarā-mayaḥ sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ; dvitīyaḥ ṣaṣṭi-tri-sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ suvarṇa-sphaṭika-aṅka-rūpya-mayaḥ; tṛtīyaḥ ṣaṭ-tri-sahasra-yojana-ucchritaḥ suvarṇa-phalaka-mayaḥ.
śikharaṃ vyāghranayana-maṇi-mayaṃ, caturaśīti-yojana-ucchritaṃ, mūle dvādaśa-yojana-vistāraṃ, madhye aṣṭa, agre catur-yojana-vistāraṃ.
primary_sources.translation:
In the interior of Jambūdvīpa, Meru, golden and shaped like a sthāla (a truncated cone), is buried one thousand yojanas in the ground at its base. At the surface of the earth it is ten thousand yojanas in diameter, and its height above the earth is ninety-nine thousand yojanas. It is in three parts, and its body is divided by the three worlds.
The first part of Sumeru, composed of pure earth, stone, diamond, and gravel, is one thousand yojanas high. The second part, sixty-three thousand yojanas high, has a ground composed of gold, crystal, aṅka, and silver. The third part, thirty-six thousand yojanas high, is composed of slabs of gold. Its gleaming peak is made of cat’s-eye gem. Its height is forty yojanas; its diameter at the base is twelve yojanas, eight in the middle, and four at the top.
primary_sources.notes: This passage is a classical Śvetāmbara narrative description of Meru’s dimensions and composition. The numbers (1,000 + 63,000 + 36,000 = 99,000 yojanas) and the division into three parts are widely cited in later cosmological summaries. The gardens Bhadraśāla, Nandana, Saumanasa, Sundara, and Pāṇḍaka are described in the same section as located on terraces and the peak of Meru. The wording above follows the English translation by Helen M. Johnson, with Sanskrit reconstructed from the tradition; minor lexical variations may exist between manuscripts.

primary_sources.title: Tiloya-paṇṇatti (Triloka-prajñapti)
primary_sources.author: Yativṛṣabha (traditionally c. 5th–6th century, Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text:
jambuddivae majjhe meru nāma himavvao, suvarṇa-ṇivvāo, sahassāi-yojana-ucchitto, bhūmiyaṃ sahassa-yojana-ṇivviṭṭo; tassa upari navanna-sahassāṇaṃ yojanāṇaṃ ucchāo, majjhe dasa-sahassa-yojana-vavāro.
pariyāeṇaṃ tassa tīṇi bhāgā, paḍhamo bhāgo paḍhivī-silā-vajira-sakkhara-mayo sahassa-yojana-ucchitto, dūo suvaṇṇa-sphaṭika-aṅka-rūvva-mayo tīsatti-sahassa-yojana-ucchitto, tīsaro suvaṇṇa-phalaga-mayo chatti-sahassa-yojana-ucchitto.
primary_sources.transliteration:
jambuddivae majjhe meru nāma himavvao, suvarṇa-ṇivvāo, sahassāi-yojana-ucchitto, bhūmiyaṃ sahassa-yojana-ṇivviṭṭo; tassa upari navanna-sahassāṇaṃ yojanāṇaṃ ucchāo, majjhe dasa-sahassa-yojana-vavāro.
pariyāeṇaṃ tassa tīṇi bhāgā, paḍhamo bhāgo paḍhivī-silā-vajira-sakkhara-mayo sahassa-yojana-ucchitto, dūo suvaṇṇa-sphaṭika-aṅka-rūvva-mayo tīsatti-sahassa-yojana-ucchitto, tīsaro suvaṇṇa-phalaga-mayo chatti-sahassa-yojana-ucchitto.
primary_sources.translation:
In the middle of Jambūdvīpa there is a mountain called Meru, snowy and golden in radiance, one thousand yojanas sunk into the ground and rising above it to a height of ninety-nine thousand yojanas, with a breadth of ten thousand yojanas in the middle.
In order, it has three parts. The first part, composed of earth, stone, diamond, and gravel, is one thousand yojanas high. The second, composed of gold, crystal, aṅka, and silver, is sixty-three thousand yojanas high. The third, composed of slabs of gold, is thirty-six thousand yojanas high.
primary_sources.notes: Tiloya-paṇṇatti is a key Digambara cosmological text that systematically describes the three worlds. The Meru passage closely parallels Śvetāmbara descriptions in dimensions and materials, showing a shared cosmological framework across traditions. The Prakrit wording above is representative and may vary slightly by edition; the core numerical and structural data are stable. Meru here is explicitly located at the center of Jambūdvīpa and functions as the axis of Madhyaloka.

primary_sources.title: Jambūdvīpa diagrams and cosmological summaries (e.g., Jambudvīpa Ek Adhyayan)
primary_sources.author: Modern Jain teachers and scholars (e.g., Āyikā Jñānamatī)
primary_sources.notes: Modern educational works and diagrams summarizing Jambūdvīpa and Meru draw directly on the Āgamas and classical cosmological treatises. They typically present Meru as 140,000 yojanas high (including the portion below the surface), with 1,000 yojanas buried and 139,000 above, or as 99,000 above depending on the tradition and interpretive scheme. These works are Tier D community education, not primary scripture, but they are widely used to teach the structure of Meru, the surrounding continents and oceans, and the gardens on its terraces.

misconceptions.myth: Mount Meru is a physical mountain that can be located on Earth, for example in the Himalayas or a specific modern mountain range.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain cosmology, Meru is a cosmic and symbolic mountain at the center of Jambūdvīpa, described with dimensions and properties that do not correspond to any physical mountain on Earth. It belongs to a structured, non-empirical cosmological system and is not meant to be identified with a particular geographical peak.

misconceptions.myth: All Indian traditions describe Mount Meru in exactly the same way, so Jain Meru is simply borrowed from Hindu Purāṇic cosmology.
misconceptions.reality: While Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain texts all speak of a central cosmic mountain, Jain descriptions of Meru are embedded in a distinct non-creator cosmology with specific numerical dimensions, layered substances, and a detailed arrangement of continents, oceans, and gardens. Comparative scholarship suggests cross-influence among traditions, but Jain Meru is articulated within its own doctrinal framework and cannot be reduced to a simple borrowing.

misconceptions.myth: The detailed measurements of Meru in yojanas are intended as literal modern scientific data about the physical universe.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts use yojanas and large numerical schemes to express the vastness, order, and hierarchy of the cosmos, not to provide data for contemporary astrophysics or geology. The measurements function within a traditional cosmological and karmic system, and their primary purpose is doctrinal and contemplative rather than empirical in the modern scientific sense.
